Pregnancy

Gestational diabetes: preterm birth, baby’s health and care after pregnancy

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Gestational diabetes can increase the chance of preterm birth and other complications, but a diagnosis does not predict that they will happen. Many people have healthy pregnancies and babies with appropriate care. Understanding the different risks helps you and your team plan testing, treatment, birth and the first days at home without blame or false reassurance.

What gestational diabetes means

Insulin helps the body use glucose for energy. Pregnancy increases insulin resistance; if the pancreas cannot make enough extra insulin, blood glucose rises. Gestational diabetes mellitus, or GDM, is generally diagnosed in the second or third trimester when diabetes was not clearly present before pregnancy. It often has no symptoms, so feeling well cannot replace testing.

High glucose found early may instead reveal previously unrecognised type 1, type 2 or another form of diabetes. The team needs to classify it correctly. GDM often resolves after birth, but that must be checked. Pre-existing diabetes and GDM have different histories and care needs; neither should be dismissed as automatically mild or ranked from a label alone.

Does it increase preterm birth risk?

GDM is associated with birth before 37 completed weeks. Some labour starts spontaneously; sometimes clinicians recommend earlier birth because of maternal illness, glucose problems, fetal concerns or other complications. Excess amniotic fluid can also contribute to premature labour. Recommended early delivery and spontaneous preterm labour are different pathways, not proof that glucose alone caused every early birth.

Earlier diagnosis can identify a group with greater metabolic risk or previously unrecognised diabetes. A 2026 review found higher preterm-birth risk in earlier-diagnosed groups, but studies used different definitions and were mostly observational. There is no universal point at 24 weeks after which the risk simply falls away. Your glucose pattern, blood pressure, growth, other conditions and treatment response matter more than a calendar promise.

Large babies and difficulties during birth

Maternal glucose crosses the placenta, and the fetus can respond by producing more insulin, encouraging growth. A baby may become large for gestational age or have macrosomia, but not every baby exposed to GDM is large. Ultrasound estimates have uncertainty; a predicted weight does not tell the team exactly what the birth will be like.

Greater size can increase shoulder dystocia, when the shoulders become stuck during birth, and birth injury such as nerve injury or fracture. Oxygen compromise and other serious injuries require prompt professional care, but are not inevitable. Assisted vaginal birth or caesarean may be needed in some circumstances. Discuss the benefits and risks of vaginal birth, induction and caesarean using your actual findings rather than assuming surgery is required.

Why newborn glucose can become low

After birth the placental glucose supply stops while the baby may still be producing extra insulin. This can lower the baby’s glucose, called neonatal hypoglycaemia. Babies can be at risk even when they do not look large or unwell. Newborn glucose checks use a maternity-unit protocol; an adult home meter or appearance alone cannot establish that the baby is safe.

Prematurity, breathing difficulty and low glucose can make sucking and feeding harder. Ask for early feeding support and a written plan for repeat checks. Expressed milk, supplementation, prescribed glucose gel or intravenous glucose may be needed according to the baby’s condition. These are clinical decisions; do not give a newborn sugar water, honey or medicines yourself. Feeding support and treatment can be provided together.

Jaundice and extra red blood cells

Jaundice is yellowing caused by bilirubin building up as red blood cells are broken down and the newborn liver processes it. Babies affected by diabetes can have a higher chance of jaundice, especially alongside prematurity or feeding problems. The team measures bilirubin when indicated and decides whether monitoring, feeding help or phototherapy is needed; colour alone cannot show the level.

Some infants have too many red blood cells, called polycythaemia. This can increase blood viscosity and be associated with feeding, glucose, breathing or jaundice problems, although not every affected infant has symptoms or hyperviscosity. Clinicians investigate signs and select treatment; all otherwise well infants do not need the same extra blood-test package. Neither redness nor sleepiness diagnoses this condition at home.

Breathing problems are not limited to preterm babies

Surfactant helps keep the small air spaces in the lungs open. Prematurity is a major reason a baby has too little surfactant and develops respiratory distress syndrome. Maternal diabetes can also increase this risk in a term baby, but it does not mean every baby’s lungs are immature or every breathing problem has the same cause.

A baby with fast or difficult breathing, grunting, pauses or abnormal colour needs immediate assessment. Neonatal clinicians may check oxygen, glucose, infection or other causes and provide appropriate breathing support. Prematurity, birth events and other conditions affect the outlook. Do not interpret a breathing problem as an expected harmless consequence of GDM or try to manage it by feeding through distress.

Placental function and small as well as large growth

The placenta transfers oxygen and nutrients, but GDM is not a guarantee of good placental function or a large baby. A baby can be small because of placental disease, hypertension, other maternal or fetal conditions, or simply their individual growth pattern. Placental insufficiency and growth restriction are not confined exclusively to people who had diabetes before pregnancy.

If growth is slow or other findings are concerning, the team considers the whole picture and may arrange repeat growth, fluid or blood-flow assessment. A small measurement alone does not prove placental failure, and glucose control alone cannot correct every cause. Ask what the findings mean for monitoring and birth rather than assuming that either a large or small baby confirms how well you have managed diabetes.

Risks for the mother and later health

GDM is associated with high blood pressure and pre-eclampsia, and with a greater chance of induction or caesarean in some pregnancies. Pre-eclampsia can also affect fetal growth and lead to medically recommended preterm birth. Monitoring blood pressure, urine and symptoms remains important even when glucose readings meet the agreed targets.

GDM can recur in a later pregnancy and increases the parent’s future risk of type 2 diabetes. Children exposed to GDM also have higher average risks of later metabolic problems, but genes, family environment and other factors contribute; this is not an individual prediction. Supportive family habits and follow-up are useful without assigning blame or guaranteeing prevention.

Who may need testing earlier?

Anyone can develop GDM. Tell the team about previous GDM, a previous large baby, diabetes in close relatives, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS, also now called PMOS), and any previous abnormal glucose result. Age, body size, family background and population differences may influence a local risk assessment, but none is a diagnosis or a measure of personal effort.

Multiple pregnancy and other pregnancy conditions also need individual assessment. There is no universal age-over-25 rule or one worldwide prevalence figure that predicts your risk. Some health systems test everyone, while others select testing using risk factors. Ask what applies to you, especially after previous GDM; an early normal result may still need repeating later.

Screening and diagnosis use different tests

Testing commonly takes place at 24–28 weeks, with earlier assessment when indicated. A one-hour glucose challenge can be a screening step followed by a diagnostic oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT); other systems start directly with a fasting 75-g OGTT. History and examination help plan care but cannot replace the laboratory test. Follow the specific preparation instructions you are given.

Thresholds depend on the protocol; the stated diagnostic cutoffs mean values at or above those levels. For example, NICE uses fasting 5.6 mmol/L or two-hour 7.8 mmol/L after 75 g; the ADA-supported one-step approach uses fasting 5.1, one-hour 10.0 or two-hour 8.5 mmol/L. Do not mix these with a different glucose load or home-monitoring targets. Fasting 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L), HbA1c 6.5%, or random 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) with classic symptoms can indicate overt diabetes needing clinical confirmation and classification, not a universal GDM rule.

Treatment reduces risk without guaranteeing an outcome

Care usually combines glucose monitoring, individual nutrition advice, suitable activity and medication when needed. Ask when to measure, how to record results, your own targets and whom to contact for readings outside them. Avoid skipping meals, extreme carbohydrate restriction or weight-loss diets during pregnancy. Practical support for food access, work, language or distress is part of care.

Needing medicine is not failure: insulin resistance can rise as pregnancy progresses. ADA guidance prefers insulin when medication is needed; NICE also uses metformin in selected GDM care. Placental transfer, benefits, uncertainties and your circumstances guide the choice. Do not start, stop or change doses, use herbal glucose remedies, or take aspirin just because of this article. Obtain a written plan for illness, low glucose and missed meals.

Planning birth and the baby’s first checks

Timing, place and mode of birth depend on glucose control, medicines, fetal growth, maternal conditions and local guidance. GDM alone does not require caesarean or preterm delivery. Ask why earlier birth is proposed and how its benefits balance the consequences of prematurity. Plan a setting with the newborn assessment and treatment your baby may need.

The team plans glucose management during labour and checks the baby after birth, including glucose and feeding. If both are well, staying together and skin-to-skin contact can support feeding; illness may require neonatal care. Extra tests are selected for findings such as jaundice or breathing difficulty. Discharge depends on stable glucose, effective feeding and clinical wellbeing, with clear follow-up and contact instructions rather than a guaranteed stay length.

Breastfeeding and follow-up after pregnancy

Breastfeeding is supported with diabetes; high maternal glucose does not make the milk poisonous. Ask for help with positioning, milk expression or supplementation if needed, and have medicines checked for breastfeeding. Insulin requirements can drop rapidly after birth, so follow the team’s revised plan. If insulin is still required, feeding can increase low-glucose risk and doses or food arrangements may need adjustment.

Book postnatal testing even if you feel well: ADA recommends a 75-g OGTT at 4–12 weeks; NICE generally uses fasting glucose at 6–13 weeks, with a different later-test pathway. Follow your local plan, then ongoing screening, commonly every 1–3 years or annually in UK care. Persistent high glucose needs classification rather than an automatic type 2 label. Discuss future pregnancy testing and sustainable activity and nutrition; breastfeeding and healthy habits may reduce risks but cannot guarantee that either parent or child will avoid diabetes.

When the pregnant or postpartum parent needs help

Contact your diabetes or maternity team urgently if glucose remains high despite the agreed plan, you are unwell, vomiting or unable to manage food and fluids, or you have repeated low readings. Seek immediate maternity advice for reduced or changed usual fetal movements, vaginal bleeding, suspected waters breaking or preterm labour. Severe headache, visual changes, pain below the ribs, sudden swelling or feeling very unwell need immediate assessment during pregnancy or after birth. Do not wait for the next appointment or use a home Doppler for reassurance.

Get emergency help for suspected ketoacidosis with symptoms such as vomiting, deep breathing, fruity breath, drowsiness or confusion, or for seizure, fainting or loss of consciousness. Severe, worsening, or movement- or touch-provoked abdominal/pelvic pain, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or new confusion, also needs emergency care. Heavy vaginal bleeding in pregnancy is an emergency on its own. Do not drive yourself; ask someone to take you or call an ambulance. If someone cannot swallow safely or is unconscious, give nothing by mouth and follow trained emergency advice.

When a newborn needs help

Tell the maternity or newborn team promptly if feeding is ineffective or the baby is unusually sleepy, jittery or increasingly jaundiced; these signs need assessment, not an assumption of low glucose. Jaundice in the first 24 hours requires immediate emergency assessment. So does jaundice with unusual sleepiness or difficulty waking, not feeding, floppiness, stiffness or jerking movements, a temperature of 38°C or higher or 36°C or lower, feeling abnormally hot or cold or shivering, no wet nappies, or breathing difficulty. These are alternative warning signs; do not wait for all of them. Later new or worsening jaundice, dark urine or pale stools need urgent clinical advice.

Get emergency help now for breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour, unusual pallor or mottling, cold or clammy skin, fainting, difficulty waking, seizure, or a weak, high-pitched or continuous cry. In a baby under three months, temperature 38°C or higher, temperature below 36°C, or no urine for 12 hours also needs immediate emergency assessment. Do not wait for a glucose reading or a scheduled feed, and do not drive yourself; arrange another driver or an ambulance. Not all signs need to be present.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask your team to name the glucose test and criteria used, your individual monitoring targets and the contact route for illness or readings outside the plan.

Discuss what growth, blood pressure and glucose findings mean for birth, newborn glucose checks and feeding support; ask for written instructions before discharge.

Book postpartum testing before leaving maternity care, check medicines and feeding arrangements, and agree ongoing diabetes screening and future-pregnancy assessment.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you organise clinician-provided glucose targets and readings, medicines, symptoms, feeding notes and questions for appointments. It cannot diagnose GDM or newborn hypoglycaemia, interpret an OGTT, prescribe insulin, assess placental function or decide when to give birth. Recording information must never delay contact for illness, changed movements or an unwell baby.

When to seek help

Follow your own glucose and illness plan. High readings with illness or repeated lows need urgent team advice. Changed usual movements, pregnancy bleeding, fluid loss or pre-eclampsia symptoms need immediate maternity contact. Suspected ketoacidosis, seizure, fainting/loss of consciousness, heavy pregnancy bleeding, severe/worsening/movement- or touch-provoked pelvic pain, or pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or new confusion need emergency care. Give nothing by mouth to someone who cannot swallow safely. A baby with breathing difficulty, blue/grey or unusually pale/mottled colour, cold or clammy skin, difficulty waking, seizure or weak/high-pitched/continuous cry needs emergency assessment; so does a baby under three months with 38°C or higher, below 36°C, or no urine for 12 hours. First-day jaundice or jaundice with poor feeding or illness also requires immediate emergency assessment. Do not drive yourself, arrange another driver or ambulance, and do not delay help for a glucose reading or app entry.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • GDM raises average risks of preterm birth and other complications, but does not determine your baby’s outcome.
  • Newborn growth, glucose, feeding, jaundice and breathing need appropriate assessment; a reassuring appearance alone is insufficient.
  • Screening protocols, diagnostic thresholds and home-monitoring targets are different; use the plan from your own team.
  • Nutrition, activity, medication and follow-up reduce risk, with practical support and no blame when medicine is needed.
  • Postnatal testing and future screening remain important even after normal readings; urgent symptoms must not wait.

Frequently asked questions

Can gestational diabetes lead to preterm birth?

It is associated with birth before 37 weeks, through spontaneous labour or a medically recommended early birth. Earlier diagnosis can identify greater risk, but 24 weeks is not a universal safety boundary. Your team considers glucose, blood pressure, growth and other findings.

What glucose number diagnoses GDM?

There is no single number for every test. A 75-g OGTT, a two-step challenge-plus-OGTT pathway and home readings use different criteria. NICE and ADA thresholds also differ. Fasting 126 mg/dL, HbA1c 6.5% or symptomatic random 200 mg/dL may indicate overt diabetes rather than the usual GDM thresholds; a clinician must interpret and, when needed, confirm the result.

What complications can affect the mother?

High blood pressure, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth and a greater chance of induction or caesarean are possible. Later GDM recurrence and type 2 diabetes risk also increase. None is inevitable; glucose care, blood-pressure checks and postpartum follow-up all matter.

Can placental problems happen with GDM?

Yes. GDM does not exclude placental disease or growth restriction, which have several causes. Nor does a small baby automatically prove placental failure. The team assesses growth, blood pressure and other findings and selects additional monitoring.

Does a baby always have low glucose or breathing problems?

No. These are risks, not guaranteed outcomes. Glucose may fall when maternal supply stops but infant insulin remains high. Prematurity and diabetes can contribute to respiratory distress. Appropriate newborn checks and feeding support help identify and treat problems.

Will I need medicine or a caesarean?

That depends on your readings and clinical circumstances. Medicine can be needed despite careful food choices and activity. Birth decisions also depend on growth, maternal health and local guidance; GDM alone is not an automatic indication for surgery or preterm birth.

Can I breastfeed, and do I still need a postnatal test?

Breastfeeding is supported, with medicine and low-glucose plans reviewed. A postnatal test is still needed: for example, ADA uses a 75-g OGTT at 4–12 weeks, whereas NICE generally uses fasting glucose at 6–13 weeks. Ongoing screening and future pregnancy planning remain important.

Which symptoms should not wait?

Get immediate maternity advice for changed usual movements, bleeding, fluid loss or pre-eclampsia symptoms. Suspected ketoacidosis, seizure, loss of consciousness, heavy pregnancy bleeding or severe, worsening or movement/touch-provoked pelvic pain need emergency care; pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or new confusion also qualifies. A baby with breathing difficulty, abnormal colour, cold or clammy skin, difficulty waking, seizure or abnormal cry needs emergency help; so does a baby under three months with 38°C or higher, below 36°C, or no urine for 12 hours. Do not drive yourself or delay for a reading.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
